A complete workflow

Written by Mohammed Saqr and Sonsoles López-Pernas

Source: vignettes/articles/workflow.Rmd
workflow.Rmd

Lag sequential analysis (LSA) asks whether one event follows another more often, or less often, than it would if the events of a sequence were independent of each other (Bakeman & Gottman, 1997; Bakeman & Quera, 2011). For every ordered pair of states it compares the observed count of the transition with the count expected from the marginal frequencies of the two states, and expresses the difference as an adjusted residual: a positive residual marks a transition the process favours, a negative residual marks a transition the process avoids.

A finding from LSA is a claim, and each kind of claim needs its own evidence. A descriptive claim (“disengaged students tend to stay disengaged”) rests on the fitted transition table. A claim about a single transition adds an interval for it. A claim about the whole network adds a check that the network reproduces in independent halves of the data. A claim that two groups differ needs a test of the difference. This guide runs that chain from end to end on the bundled data: it fits a model to weekly engagement states, reads and draws the result, adds uncertainty evidence, then fits one model per achievement group from a raw event log and tests where the groups differ. The method itself is introduced in the LSA vignette; the full confirmatory battery is in the confirmatory vignette.

library(lagdynamics)

Data

The first part of the guide uses engagement, a wide data frame with one row per student and one column per week of a course.

  • Sequence: each row is one student; 138 rows, of which 2 are empty.
  • Time point: the 15 columns, in course order.
  • State: the weekly engagement state, Active, Average, or Disengaged. A missing cell means no record that week.
head(engagement)
#>         1          2          3          4          5          6       7       8       9
#> 1  Active Disengaged Disengaged Disengaged     Active     Active  Active  Active Average
#> 2 Average    Average    Average    Average    Average    Average Average Average Average
#> 3 Average     Active     Active     Active     Active     Active  Active  Active  Active
#> 4  Active     Active     Active     Active     Active    Average Average  Active  Active
#> 5  Active     Active     Active    Average     Active    Average  Active  Active  Active
#> 6 Average    Average Disengaged    Average Disengaged Disengaged Average Average Average
#>           10      11         12      13      14      15
#> 1     Active Average     Active    <NA>    <NA>    <NA>
#> 2     Active Average    Average Average Average Average
#> 3    Average  Active     Active  Active  Active  Active
#> 4     Active Average     Active Average  Active Average
#> 5 Disengaged  Active     Active  Active Average Average
#> 6 Disengaged Average Disengaged Average Average Average

The second part uses group_regulation_long, an event log of collaborative learning with one coded regulation action per row.

  • Actor: Actor, the student who acted; 2,000 actors.
  • Action: Action, one of nine regulation codes (adapt, cohesion, consensus, coregulate, discuss, emotion, monitor, plan, synthesis).
  • Time: Time, the time stamp that orders the actions.
  • Group: Achiever, High or Low achievement, fixed for each actor.
head(group_regulation_long)
#>   Actor Achiever Group Course                Time    Action
#> 1     1     High     1      A 2025-01-01 08:27:07  cohesion
#> 2     1     High     1      A 2025-01-01 08:35:20 consensus
#> 3     1     High     1      A 2025-01-01 08:42:18   discuss
#> 4     1     High     1      A 2025-01-01 08:50:00 synthesis
#> 5     1     High     1      A 2025-01-01 08:52:25     adapt
#> 6     1     High     1      A 2025-01-01 08:57:31 consensus

Fit the model

lsa() turns the rows into sequences, counts every lag-1 transition, computes the counts expected under independence, and tests each cell. The print method gives the size of the data, the tablewise independence test, and the strongest favoured transitions.

fit <- lsa(engagement)
fit
#> Lag Sequential Analysis  -  classical  (lag 1, directed)
#>   3 states | 1734 transitions | 1870 events | 136 sequences
#>   states: Active, Average, Disengaged
#>   independence: G² = 618.3, df = 4, p <2e-16
#> 
#>   Significant transitions (p < 0.05): 7 of 9
#>   strongest over-represented (of 3):
#>     Active -> Active          z =  +21.7  ***
#>     Disengaged -> Disengaged  z =  +15.4  ***
#>     Average -> Average        z =  +12.5  ***
#> 
#>   Initial states:
#>     Active     0.382  ████████████████████████
#>     Average    0.368  ███████████████████████
#>     Disengaged 0.250  ████████████████

The model rests on 1,734 transitions from 136 sequences: the two empty rows contribute nothing. The likelihood-ratio test of independence is G² = 618.3 on 4 degrees of freedom, so the weekly states are far from independent of the previous week’s state. Seven of the nine transitions depart from chance, and the three favoured ones are the three self-transitions: Active -> Active (z = 21.7), Disengaged -> Disengaged (z = 15.4), and Average -> Average (z = 12.5). Engagement is persistent.

Overview of the fit

summary() returns the same overview as one table row, and the nodes table describes the states: how many transitions leave and enter each state, their shares, and the share of sequences that start in it.

as.data.frame(summary(fit))
#>      engine lag n_states n_sequences n_events n_transitions n_significant alpha lrx2
#> 1 classical   1        3         136     1870          1734             7  0.05  618
#>   lrx2_df    lrx2_p  x2 x2_df      x2_p
#> 1       4 1.69e-132 629     4 7.41e-135
as.data.frame(summary(fit), what = "nodes")
#>        state outgoing incoming out_share in_share init_prob
#> 1     Active      658      651     0.379    0.375     0.382
#> 2    Average      751      763     0.433    0.440     0.368
#> 3 Disengaged      325      320     0.187    0.185     0.250

Average carries the largest share of activity (0.433 of outgoing transitions), Disengaged the smallest (0.187). A quarter of the students (0.250) start the course disengaged, against 0.382 who start active.

Which transitions depart from chance

transitions() returns one row per transition, with the observed and expected counts, the transition probability, the adjusted residual and its p-value, and effect sizes (Yule’s Q, kappa, lift). sort = "strength" orders the rows by the absolute residual; significant = TRUE would keep only the transitions significant at alpha = 0.05.

transitions(fit, sort = "strength")
#>         from         to lag count expected  prob prob_col adj_res         p yules_q
#> 1     Active     Active   1   459      247 0.698   0.7051  21.663 4.60e-104   0.828
#> 2 Disengaged Disengaged   1   157       60 0.483   0.4906  15.390  1.90e-53   0.754
#> 3    Average     Active   1   153      282 0.204   0.2350 -12.906  4.16e-38  -0.601
#> 4     Active Disengaged   1    23      121 0.035   0.0719 -12.557  3.64e-36  -0.826
#> 5    Average    Average   1   458      330 0.610   0.6003  12.453  1.35e-35   0.553
#> 6     Active    Average   1   176      290 0.267   0.2307 -11.319  1.06e-29  -0.534
#> 7 Disengaged     Active   1    39      122 0.120   0.0599 -10.549  5.11e-26  -0.698
#> 8 Disengaged    Average   1   129      143 0.397   0.1691  -1.736  8.25e-02  -0.108
#> 9    Average Disengaged   1   140      139 0.186   0.4375   0.176  8.60e-01   0.011
#>     kappa kappa_z  kappa_p  lift  sign significant
#> 1  0.4438   19.19 4.68e-82 1.858  over        TRUE
#> 2  0.3136   13.56 7.34e-42 2.618  over        TRUE
#> 3 -0.4994  -14.70 6.81e-49 0.543 under        TRUE
#> 4 -0.8272  -13.41 5.14e-41 0.189 under        TRUE
#> 5  0.2275    9.83 7.97e-23 1.386  over        TRUE
#> 6 -0.4242  -12.48 9.39e-36 0.608 under        TRUE
#> 7 -0.7069  -11.46 2.03e-30 0.320 under        TRUE
#> 8 -0.1618   -2.96 3.03e-03 0.902 under       FALSE
#> 9 -0.0903   -1.66 9.79e-02 1.010  over       FALSE

Four of the six moves between different states are avoided. The strongest avoidance is Average -> Active (z = -12.9, Yule’s Q = -0.601), followed closely by Active -> Disengaged (z = -12.6): an active student almost never drops to disengagement in one week (23 observed against 121 expected, probability 0.035). The remaining two moves, Disengaged -> Average (z = -1.74, p = 0.083) and Average -> Disengaged (z = 0.18, p = 0.86), occur about as often as chance predicts. The probability column is the transition probability that a transition network displays; the residual and Yule’s Q say whether that probability is larger or smaller than chance.

Display the model

A residual heatmap shows the residual of every cell: rows are the current state, columns the next state, and the colour gives the sign and size of the departure from chance.

plot(fit)

The three red cells are the self-transitions and the blue cells the avoided moves between states, which is the persistence reported above in one display. The rows are ordered by how many transitions leave each state, so the self-transitions do not form a visual diagonal.

A transition network draws the same process with edges weighted by transition probability, the form used in transition network analysis. It answers a different question: where the process tends to go next, rather than which moves are surprising.

plot(fit, type = "network", weights = "tna")

The two displays answer different questions, and they part ways on Disengaged -> Average: with a probability of 0.397 it is one of the heaviest edges in the transition network, yet its residual is not significant, because Average is common enough that chance alone predicts a move of that size. Every display is covered in the plotting guide.

How precise are the transition probabilities

certainty_lsa() gives analytic credible intervals for each transition probability from a Dirichlet-multinomial posterior, and marks an edge as stable when its residual keeps its sign across the interval.

cert <- certainty_lsa(fit)
cert
#> <lsa_certainty>  (analytic Dirichlet-Multinomial)
#>   engine:        classical
#>   prior:         Dirichlet(0.50)
#>   CI level:      95%  |  inference: stability
#>   certain edges: 7 of 9
transitions(cert, sort = "strength")
#>         from         to observed prob_observed prob_mean prob_se prob_ci_low prob_ci_high
#> 1     Active     Active      459         0.698    0.6967 0.01789      0.6611        0.731
#> 2 Disengaged Disengaged      157         0.483    0.4824 0.02761      0.4284        0.537
#> 3    Average     Active      153         0.204    0.2040 0.01468      0.1760        0.233
#> 4     Active Disengaged       23         0.035    0.0356 0.00721      0.0229        0.051
#> 5    Average    Average      458         0.610    0.6093 0.01777      0.5742        0.644
#> 6     Active    Average      176         0.267    0.2676 0.01723      0.2345        0.302
#> 7 Disengaged     Active       39         0.120    0.1210 0.01802      0.0879        0.158
#> 8 Disengaged    Average      129         0.397    0.3966 0.02703      0.3443        0.450
#> 9    Average Disengaged      140         0.186    0.1867 0.01420      0.1597        0.215
#>    p_value stable adj_res_observed adj_res_stable
#> 1 5.56e-20   TRUE           21.663           TRUE
#> 2 9.44e-06   TRUE           15.390           TRUE
#> 3 6.06e-04   TRUE          -12.906           TRUE
#> 4 2.19e-01  FALSE          -12.557          FALSE
#> 5 3.14e-17   TRUE           12.453           TRUE
#> 6 1.21e-04   TRUE          -11.319           TRUE
#> 7 9.45e-02  FALSE          -10.549          FALSE
#> 8 2.23e-04   TRUE           -1.736           TRUE
#> 9 1.17e-03   TRUE            0.176           TRUE

Seven of the nine probabilities are certain. The probability of the strongest edge, Active -> Active, lies between 0.661 and 0.731 with 95% credibility. The two uncertain ones are the two rarest transitions, Active -> Disengaged (23 observations, interval 0.023 to 0.051) and Disengaged -> Active (39 observations): their intervals are wide relative to the probability itself, so the posterior does not stay within 75% to 125% of the observed value. Their residuals are strongly negative all the same; the uncertainty concerns the size of a small probability, not the avoidance.

Do the residuals hold when sequences are resampled

bootstrap_lsa() resamples whole sequences with replacement, refits the model on each resample, and reports a percentile interval for every statistic (Efron, 1979). Resampling sequences keeps each student’s transitions together, so the interval reflects variation between students. The seed makes the resamples reproducible.

set.seed(2026)
boot <- bootstrap_lsa(fit, R = 1000)
boot
#> <lsa_bootstrap>
#>   engine:        classical
#>   level:         sequence
#>   replicates:    1000
#>   CI level:      95%
#>   stable edges:  7 of 9
transitions(boot, significant = TRUE, sort = "strength") |> head(5)
#>         from         to observed count_mean count_se count_ci_low count_ci_high
#> 1     Active     Active      459      461.1    52.50          360           568
#> 2 Disengaged Disengaged      157      156.1    28.06          106           213
#> 3    Average     Active      153      152.8    14.79          124           182
#> 4     Active Disengaged       23       22.7     4.99           14            32
#> 5    Average    Average      458      458.8    39.30          383           532
#>   adj_res_observed adj_res_mean adj_res_se adj_res_ci_low adj_res_ci_high adj_res_p_boot
#> 1             21.7         21.6       1.55          18.65           24.61              0
#> 2             15.4         15.3       1.96          11.10           18.95              0
#> 3            -12.9        -12.9       1.52         -15.79           -9.99              0
#> 4            -12.6        -12.5       1.06         -14.68          -10.42              0
#> 5             12.5         12.5       1.37           9.84           15.16              0
#>   adj_res_stable prob_observed prob_mean prob_ci_low prob_ci_high yules_q_observed
#> 1           TRUE         0.698    0.6974      0.6371        0.752            0.828
#> 2           TRUE         0.483    0.4800      0.3846        0.564            0.754
#> 3           TRUE         0.204    0.2041      0.1623        0.247           -0.601
#> 4           TRUE         0.035    0.0346      0.0205        0.049           -0.826
#> 5           TRUE         0.610    0.6102      0.5640        0.655            0.553
#>   yules_q_mean yules_q_ci_low yules_q_ci_high
#> 1        0.826          0.760           0.882
#> 2        0.750          0.633           0.834
#> 3       -0.601         -0.700          -0.489
#> 4       -0.826         -0.900          -0.745
#> 5        0.553          0.451           0.648

Seven of the nine residuals are stable across 1,000 resamples of students, and every interval shown excludes zero by a wide margin: the residual of Active -> Disengaged stays between -14.7 and -10.4, so the avoidance of that move holds across students even though its probability is small. The persistence findings and the avoided moves are therefore not produced by a few unusual students.

Is the whole network reproducible

reliability_lsa() splits the sequences into two random halves, fits the model to each half, and correlates the two sets of edge weights. A high split-half correlation means the network as a whole would be recovered from a different sample of the same size.

rel <- reliability_lsa(fit, R = 100)
rel
#> <lsa_reliability>
#>   engine:        classical
#>   replicates:    100
#>   weights:       prob
#>   method:        pearson
#>   n sequences:   136
#>   split-half r:  0.961  (sd = 0.034)
#>   95% CI:        [0.890, 0.993]
#>   failed:        0 of 100 replicates

Across 100 random splits the two halves agree closely: the mean split-half correlation is 0.961, with a 95% interval from 0.890 to 0.993, and no split failed. The engagement network is reproducible at this sample size.

From an event log to sequences

Process data usually arrives as an event log rather than as wide sequences. lsa() builds the sequences itself when the columns are named: actor identifies the sequence, action is the state, and time orders the events. A new sequence also starts whenever two consecutive events of an actor are more than time_threshold seconds apart (900 by default). The column grammar and its options are covered in the event-log guide.

fit_log <- lsa(group_regulation_long, actor = "Actor", action = "Action",
               time = "Time")
fit_log
#> Lag Sequential Analysis  -  classical  (lag 1, directed)
#>   9 states | 25533 transitions | 27533 events | 2000 sequences
#>   states: adapt, cohesion, consensus, coregulate, discuss, emotion, monitor, plan, synthesis
#>   independence: G² = 13203.8, df = 64, p <2e-16
#> 
#>   Significant transitions (p < 0.05): 72 of 81
#>   strongest over-represented (of 23):
#>     emotion -> cohesion      z =  +58.2  ***
#>     discuss -> synthesis     z =  +48.0  ***
#>     synthesis -> adapt       z =  +38.8  ***
#>     consensus -> coregulate  z =  +35.3  ***
#>     consensus -> plan        z =  +32.6  ***
#>     ... and 18 more
#> 
#>   Initial states:
#>     consensus  0.214  ████████████████████████
#>     plan       0.204  ███████████████████████
#>     discuss    0.175  ████████████████████
#>     emotion    0.151  █████████████████
#>     monitor    0.144  ████████████████
#>     cohesion   0.060  ███████
#>     synthesis  0.019  ██
#>     coregulate 0.019  ██
#>     adapt      0.011  █

The 27,533 actions form 2,000 sequences, one per actor, and 25,533 transitions. Seventy-two of the 81 transitions depart from chance. The strongest favoured transition is emotion -> cohesion (z = 58.2), followed by discuss -> synthesis (z = 48.0).

One model per group

Naming a grouping column with group fits one model per group under the same set of states. The grouping column must be constant within each sequence.

gfit <- lsa(group_regulation_long, actor = "Actor", action = "Action",
            time = "Time", group = "Achiever")
summary(gfit)
#>   group    engine lag n_states n_sequences n_events n_transitions n_significant alpha
#> 1  High classical   1        9        1000    13721         12721            66  0.05
#> 2   Low classical   1        9        1000    13812         12812            67  0.05
#>   lrx2 lrx2_df lrx2_p   x2 x2_df x2_p
#> 1 6147      64      0 6807    64    0
#> 2 7715      64      0 9197    64    0

Each group contributes 1,000 sequences: 12,721 transitions for the high achievers and 12,812 for the low achievers. Both tables reject independence, and the groups have a similar number of significant transitions (66 and 67). Every reading verb returns a leading group column for a grouped fit.

transitions(gfit, significant = TRUE, sort = "strength") |> head(6)
#>   group      from         to lag count expected   prob prob_col adj_res         p yules_q
#> 1  High   emotion   cohesion   1   505    114.0 0.3258  0.53953    40.6  0.00e+00   0.847
#> 2  High consensus  consensus   1   283    917.0 0.0834  0.08229   -28.6 3.68e-180  -0.698
#> 3  High   discuss  synthesis   1   213     46.1 0.1063  0.72696    27.1 1.79e-161   0.881
#> 4  High   discuss       plan   1    25    458.8 0.0125  0.00858   -25.1 2.35e-139  -0.934
#> 5  High consensus coregulate   1   580    254.4 0.1710  0.60797    24.8 1.21e-135   0.663
#> 6  High consensus       plan   1  1236    777.0 0.3644  0.42416    21.9 2.64e-106   0.447
#>    kappa kappa_z   kappa_p   lift  sign significant
#> 1  0.425    37.7 6.36e-311 4.4280  over        TRUE
#> 2 -0.709   -30.1 5.36e-199 0.3086 under        TRUE
#> 3  0.613    25.5 5.39e-143 4.6169  over        TRUE
#> 4 -0.949   -26.0 3.81e-149 0.0545 under        TRUE
#> 5  0.462    24.6 9.79e-134 2.2801  over        TRUE
#> 6  0.180    19.0  3.49e-80 1.5907  over        TRUE

The strongest residual in the high achievers is emotion -> cohesion (z = 40.6). The question of the next section is whether any transition is stronger in one group than in the other.

Do the groups differ

compare_lsa() tests the difference between the groups edge by edge. The statistic is the difference in the log odds ratio of each transition between the groups; its null distribution comes from permuting the group labels of whole sequences, R times. With many edges tested at once, the p-values are corrected for multiplicity: adjust = "BH" applies the Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate correction, and the significant column below refers to the adjusted p-values (p_adj). The package default is no adjustment, so the argument is passed explicitly.

set.seed(2026)
cmp <- compare_lsa(gfit, R = 1000, adjust = "BH")
cmp
#> <lsa_comparison>
#>   groups:   High vs Low
#>   measure:  log_or difference (High - Low)
#>   R:        1000 label permutations
#>   edges:    39 significant of 78 tested (adjust = BH)
#>   omnibus:  statistic = 79.48, p = 0.000999
as.data.frame(cmp, what = "global")
#>   group_a group_b statistic  p_value    R
#> 1    High     Low      79.5 0.000999 1000

The omnibus test rejects the hypothesis that the two groups share one transition structure (statistic 79.5, p = 0.000999). That p-value is 1 / (R + 1), the smallest value 1,000 permutations can give, so the difference is at least as extreme as the permutation null allows. Of the 78 edges with enough observations to test (the default min_count = 5), 39 differ after the Benjamini-Hochberg correction. Sorting by the size of the difference shows the largest ones.

transitions(cmp, significant = TRUE, sort = "strength") |> head(8)
#>        from         to log_or_a log_or_b  diff   p_perm   p_adj significant
#> 1  cohesion      adapt   -0.794   -3.921  3.13 0.000999 0.00354        TRUE
#> 2   emotion  synthesis   -1.619   -4.522  2.90 0.000999 0.00354        TRUE
#> 3      plan  synthesis   -2.145   -4.951  2.81 0.001998 0.00577        TRUE
#> 4  cohesion  synthesis   -1.355   -3.945  2.59 0.005994 0.01461        TRUE
#> 5 synthesis    monitor   -3.229   -0.975 -2.25 0.008991 0.02063        TRUE
#> 6 synthesis       plan   -0.581   -2.680  2.10 0.000999 0.00354        TRUE
#> 7     adapt coregulate   -3.146   -1.176 -1.97 0.013986 0.02871        TRUE
#> 8      plan      adapt   -2.338   -4.230  1.89 0.024975 0.04995        TRUE

The diff column is the high-achiever log odds ratio minus the low-achiever one. The largest difference is cohesion -> adapt (3.13): the move is avoided in both groups but far more strongly by the low achievers (-3.921 against -0.794). Three of the next differences end in synthesis (emotion, plan, and cohesion -> synthesis), each avoided much more strongly by the low achievers. The negative differences run the other way: synthesis -> monitor (-2.25) is avoided more strongly by the high achievers.

A comparison barrel plot shows the two groups side by side for the most frequent transitions: the high achievers’ transition probability runs to the left and the low achievers’ to the right, the bar labels give the counts, the fill gives the log odds ratio, and the centre carries the adjusted p-value of the difference.

plot(cmp)

Seven of the twelve most frequent transitions differ between the groups. The high achievers move between discussion and consensus far more often (discuss -> consensus: 851 against 418 observations; consensus -> discuss: 789 against 401), while the low achievers more often follow discussion with synthesis (discuss -> synthesis: 344 against 213). The backbone transition consensus -> plan is equally frequent in both groups (p = 0.104).

When to use which

Claim Evidence Call
The process is not memoryless Tablewise G² test lsa(), tests()
This transition is favoured or avoided Adjusted residual transitions(fit, significant = TRUE)
The transition probability is known to this precision Credible interval certainty_lsa()
The residual holds across students Sequence bootstrap bootstrap_lsa()
The network would reproduce in new data Split-half correlation reliability_lsa()
The groups differ on this transition Permutation test, BH-adjusted compare_lsa(adjust = "BH")

Descriptive claims use the fitted tables and the displays. A claim about one edge adds an interval, a claim about the whole network adds reliability, and a claim about groups adds the permutation comparison with the multiplicity correction stated.

References

Bakeman, R., & Gottman, J. M. (1997). Observing interaction: An introduction to sequential analysis (2nd ed.). Cambridge University Press.

Bakeman, R., & Quera, V. (2011). Sequential analysis and observational methods for the behavioral sciences. Cambridge University Press.

Efron, B. (1979). Bootstrap methods: Another look at the jackknife. The Annals of Statistics, 7(1), 1-26.
